milestone.title: Microsoft's Windows reaches the computer press
milestone.note: The November 21 InfoWorld demonstration captured Microsoft's first public bid to make a graphical, mouse-driven layer a standard across MS-DOS personal computers.

editorNote: A mouse, overlapping panels and a common face for DOS programs point toward a different kind of personal-computer desk.
morningLine: Microsoft opens a window on the DOS world while Thanksgiving shoppers confront a bruising home-computer price war.

lead.headline: Microsoft Opens a Window on the DOS Desktop
lead.dek: The newly announced graphical environment promises one mouse-driven face across the expanding MS-DOS market—but Microsoft is still showing a future product, not shipping one.
lead.confidence: Exact-date milestone; announcement November 10 and illustrated in the November 21 InfoWorld.
body: Microsoft has put a name and a visible face on its plan for the next stage of MS-DOS computing. Windows, announced in New York on November 10 and pictured for readers in this week’s InfoWorld, places menus, icons and movable on-screen panels between the operator and familiar programs. A mouse becomes a working tool rather than an exotic laboratory accessory.

The ambition is broader than a handsome screen. Microsoft wants a graphical environment that can travel across the growing population of DOS machines, collecting support from hardware builders and software publishers instead of belonging to a single proprietary computer. In an industry crowded with partly compatible systems, that common layer may be the most important part of the proposal.

Windows enters an active contest. VisiCorp’s Visi On is the immediate commercial benchmark, while other makers are pursuing their own graphical ideas. Microsoft says users will be able to move among applications and work through a consistent set of visual commands, a striking contrast with the command lines and memorized keystrokes now governing most desks.

Buyers should keep the calendar straight: Windows is a pre-release demonstration, not a box on this week’s store shelf. Microsoft projects shipment in April 1984. For now, the November display is a declaration of direction—an attempt to make the graphical desktop a standard companion to DOS.

stories.headline: Holiday Buyers Enter a Home-Computer Shakeout
body: The Christmas aisle is filled with bargains produced by a punishing price battle. TIME found one Atari home computer advertised in Los Angeles for $77.95, down from $630 three years earlier, while Commodore, Atari and Texas Instruments fought for volume at ever-thinner margins.

Texas Instruments has already announced its withdrawal from the home-computer business after severe losses. Clearance prices may delight shoppers, but they also raise hard questions about continued support, software and which machines will still have manufacturers behind them next year.

The cartridge-game crash deepens the uncertainty. Retailers are carrying discounted inventory, and publishers that once depended on dedicated consoles are looking toward home computers and rival platforms. The holiday bargain is real; so is the shakeout behind it.

stories.headline: IBM's PCjr Sets a $669 Floor for Big Blue at Home
stories.confidence: Same-month announcement; availability expected in early 1984.
body: IBM’s newly announced PCjr brings the company’s badge toward the family room at $669 for a 64K entry model. A $1,269 enhanced version adds 128K and a 360K disk drive, while color, sound, cartridge slots and a cordless infrared keyboard distinguish the small machine from its office-bred relative.

The Junior is not yet generally on sale; IBM points to the first quarter of 1984. Nor should buyers assume complete IBM PC software compatibility. Those cautions leave the holiday spotlight on the announcement itself and on whether IBM can stretch its business-computer authority into the fiercely priced home market.

stories.headline: Computer Chess Programs Learn to Outsmart One Another
body: Tournament programmers are setting computers against computers, turning the chessboard into a public test of search, evaluation and machine strategy. A November 21 Christian Science Monitor report follows the contests as programs expose one another’s weaknesses move by move.

Computer chess remains entertainment, experiment and demonstration at once. Every stronger performance gives home users a vivid measure of improving software, while programmers gain a demanding arena in which a bad assumption can be punished before spectators.

stories.headline: An Eyebrow-Controlled Computer Gives a Scientist His Voice
body: A paralyzed scientist in Nashville is continuing to communicate and work through a computer controlled by eyebrow movement, UPI reported November 22. The system turns a small remaining physical motion into selections and composed messages.

The achievement offers a humane counterpoint to this week’s retail battles. Personal computing is not only about speed, price or entertainment; carefully adapted input can restore a channel for thought and professional life when ordinary keyboards are impossible to use.
